newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Palestinians accuse Israel of "ethnic cleansing".
newsitem.headline: Palestinians accuse Israel of "ethnic cleansing".

text.p: Palestinian officials said on Sunday that Israeli plans to demolish 500 Palestinian houses on Israeli-occupied West Bank land amounted to a policy of "ethnic cleansing" likely to spark violence.

A senior Israeli security source said earlier that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's administration intended this year to destroy more than 500 structures built without permits on land still occupied by Israel.

Palestinian Information Minister Yasser Abed Rabbo, speaking to Israel Radio in Arabic, swiftly condemned the policy as "systematic ethnic cleansing" which could "bring about certain confrontation in the region".
An Israeli official confirmed hundreds of homes were built without permits but a spokesman insisted anyone facing the demolition of his property could still challenge the order.

"To throw out propaganda slurs without looking at the validity of each individual case is just to distort the truth," government spokesman Moshe Fogel said in response to the charge of ethnic cleansing.
Yasser Arafat's Palestinian Authority, which has taken over parts of the West Bank under a 1993 accord with Israel, views the continued Israeli occupation as itself illegal -- along with demolitions.

On Sunday, Palestinians characterised the demolition policy as another nail in the coffin of Arab-Israeli peacemaking, already faltering over Israel's expansion of Jewish settlements on occupied West Bank land.
"This hellish plan is like shooting the dead peace process with a machinegun," Arafat's adviser Ahmed Tibi told Reuters.

U.S. Middle East troubleshooter Dennis Ross left the region at the weekend after nine days of mediation attempts, and Palestinians said his mission's failure proved Washington must reshape its policies if it was to rescue the talks.

"I hope that the American administration will wake up from its deep sleep and do something about the Israeli government's kicking the Palestinians off their land and confiscating the land and now demolishing in a brutal and intensive manner their homes," Tibi said.

The Israeli security source said 80 Palestinian structures had been destroyed in the West Bank so far in 1997, while 450 had been destroyed since the signing of the landmark Israel-PLO peace accord in 1993 and 1,900 since 1988.
"The policy of the government and the defence establishment is to impose law and order and to deal with violations of the law by both Arabs and Jews," Israel's defence ministry said.

Israeli-Palestinian talks sputtered to a halt two months ago after Israeli bulldozers began carving out a Jewish settlement on a hilltop in East Jerusalem, occupied by Israel with the rest of the West Bank in the 1967 Middle East war.
Earlier this month, security forces demolished three shacks built by Jews at the Yitzhar settlement in the West Bank and removed mobile homes at another settlement.

Israel Radio said police and soldiers planned on Monday to again force settlers out of the homes in Yitzhar after residents rebuilt them. Settlers had complained authorities were focusing on Israeli violations but ignoring illegal Palestinian building.

More than 130,000 Israelis live in heavily guarded settlements scattered throughout the West Bank amid some two million Palestinians. Despite interim accords, final peace talks have yet to resume under Netanyahu who took office last June.
The European Union, following hard on the heels of Ross, pledged to redouble its efforts to resolve the crisis.

"The situation has become very dangerous," Miguel Angel Moratinos, the EU's Middle East envoy, said in Cairo before heading for Gaza on Sunday and then Israel. "The peace process must be saved," he added.

But prospects of mediating a breakthough in the peace process remained daunting, since Israel views the EU as siding firmly with the Palestinians and the Palestinians see the Clinton administration as tilting toward the Jewish state.

U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, who met Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy in Washington on Friday, said she would visit the Middle East only when the parties made the "difficult decisions" required to break the deadlock.
